title: Reasonable adjustments in hospital and community
blurb: Plan practical reasonable adjustments for people with a learning disability: timing, environment, people, preparation and information.
question: Ethan, 23, is autistic with a mild learning disability. He becomes very distressed in busy waiting rooms and left his last outpatient appointment before being seen. He needs a follow-up in clinic. Which adjustment should the nurse plan?

teach.h: Adjustments turn equal rights into equal care
teach.body: Reasonable adjustments are changes to how a service works so that a disabled person is not at a substantial disadvantage. For services they must be planned in advance and cannot be charged for. In plain English: find what makes care hard for this person, such as waiting, noise, needles, unfamiliar places or written letters, and change the service, not the person. Small changes like a first appointment of the day can be the difference between care and no care.

teach.h: Common adjustments and why they work
head: Adjustment
Barrier it removes
rows: First or last appointment of the day
Quiet waiting space or side room
teach.caption: For autistic adults NICE CG142 1.1.8 recommends adjusting personal space, visual supports, wall colours, lighting and noise; CG170 1.1.9 says the same for autistic children and young people.

teach.body: Ethan, 23, is autistic with a mild learning disability and left his last appointment because the waiting room was too busy. The nurse books the first appointment of the day, arranges a quiet place to wait or a text when the clinician is ready, sends an easy read letter with a photo of the clinic, and records these adjustments on his record and digital flag so every visit is planned the same way. Ethan is not charged for any of it.

teach.h: Learning disability liaison nurses and carers
teach.body: Hospital learning disability liaison nurses help wards plan admissions, adjust care, and support capacity and best interests processes. Contact them before a planned admission, not on the day. Family carers and paid supporters often know the person best: agreeing that they can stay, including overnight, and planning their role with them is a common and effective adjustment. Their presence does not replace the nurse's responsibility for care.

steps.label: Weeks before
steps.sub: Contact the LD liaison nurse; share the passport

steps.label: Plan the day
steps.sub: First on the list, quiet bay, carer present

steps.label: Afterwards
steps.sub: Pain plan from passport; update the record

teach.h: Making the most of one anaesthetic
items: Some people need a general anaesthetic for a procedure others have awake, such as dental work.
If the person lacks capacity, the team can consider, in their best interests, doing other needed checks under the same anaesthetic (bloods, ear examination, dental check).
Consult family and carers, and an IMCA if needed for serious treatment with no one appropriate to consult.
Plan it in advance so the right teams are present.

teach.caption: For a person with capacity who refuses, their decision is respected; desensitisation offers a way forward they can choose.

teach.text: An adjustment is about changing the service, not asking the person to cope better. 'Arrive early', 'bring two carers to keep her calm' or 'take a sedative first' all leave the barrier in place. And never charge the person for an adjustment.

items: Adjust time, place, people, preparation and information.
First or last and longer appointments; quiet spaces; attention to light and noise.
Contact the LD liaison nurse before planned admissions; let carers stay and plan their role.
Prepare with visits, social stories and graded desensitisation.
Plan ahead, record adjustments (flag, passport) and never charge for them.

summary: You can now choose practical reasonable adjustments across time, place, people, preparation and information, and plan a hospital admission with the liaison nurse and carers. You also know how desensitisation and combined procedures under one anaesthetic can help.

A.q: Ethan, 23, is autistic with a mild learning disability. He becomes very distressed in busy waiting rooms and left his last outpatient appointment before being seen. Which adjustment is most appropriate for his follow-up?
options: Ask him to arrive early to get used to the room
Book the first or last slot with a quiet place to wait
Offer a sedative to take before he leaves home
Discharge him to his GP after two missed visits
A.why: A first or last appointment and a quiet place to wait remove the barrier of busy waiting areas: a change of practice and avoidance of a physical feature under Equality Act s20(3)-(4). For autistic adults, NICE CG142 1.1.8 also supports adapting the environment.

whyNot.0: Arriving early lengthens his time in the environment that distresses him.
whyNot.2: Sedation does not remove the barrier and is not a reasonable adjustment.
whyNot.3: Discharge applies a rule that disadvantages him instead of adjusting.

A.q: Molly, 45, has a learning disability and needs a double-length dental appointment to become familiar with the room and equipment. The practice manager proposes charging her for the extra time. What is the correct position?
options: She can be charged the standard rate for the extra time
She can be charged if she has the means to pay
She must not be charged for the cost of the adjustment
Her support provider can be charged for the extra time
A.why: Equality Act s20(7): a disabled person must not be required to pay for a reasonable adjustment.

whyNot.0: Charging for the adjustment breaches s20(7).
whyNot.1: Ability to pay does not change the rule.
whyNot.3: Passing the cost to her provider avoids the practice's own duty.

A.q: Kai, 30, has a learning disability and is booked for a planned hip operation in four weeks. His community nurse wants the hospital ready with the adjustments he needs. What is the best action?
options: Contact the hospital LD liaison nurse to plan the admission
Ask Kai to explain his needs to staff on the day
Send his GP summary to the ward the day before
Wait for the ward to call if they have any questions
A.why: The learning disability liaison nurse can coordinate adjustments with the ward and theatre in advance.

whyNot.1: This leaves Kai to manage his own adjustments under stress.
whyNot.2: A GP summary the day before leaves no time to plan.
whyNot.3: Waiting for questions is not anticipatory planning.

B.q: Alys, 38, has a severe learning disability and is admitted to a medical ward. Her long-standing support worker asks to stay overnight because Alys becomes very distressed with unfamiliar people. Visiting ends at 8 pm. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Refuse, as visiting times apply to everyone
Allow it if Alys's family pay for the support worker
Allow the support worker to stay until 10 pm at most
Agree she can stay and plan her role in Alys's care
B.why: Flexible visiting so a familiar supporter can stay is a reasonable adjustment; agreeing roles makes it safe and clear.

whyNot.0: Applying the same rule to everyone can disadvantage Alys; the policy should be adjusted.
whyNot.1: Payment is not a condition of a reasonable adjustment.
whyNot.2: A partial extension does not meet her overnight need.

B.q: Tariq, 26, has a mild learning disability and capacity to decide about blood tests. He has a strong fear of needles and pulled away at his last two attempts. His GP wants routine bloods in the next few months. What is the best plan?
options: Ask two staff to hold his arm still next time
Arrange graded desensitisation with numbing cream
Ask his mother to consent to the test on his behalf
Record that he refuses and stop offering the test
B.why: Graded desensitisation, with numbing cream and preparation, helps Tariq choose to have the test. As he has capacity, holding him would be unlawful.

whyNot.0: Holding a person with capacity who refuses is unlawful.
whyNot.2: His mother cannot consent for an adult with capacity.
whyNot.3: Stopping without offering adjustments fails the duty to adjust.

B.q: Bea, 29, is autistic and has a learning disability. She attends the emergency department with a wrist injury and is rocking and covering her ears in the crowded waiting area. The wait is three hours. What is the best immediate adjustment?
options: Ask her to wait in the car park and phone her back
Move her to a quieter area while she keeps her place
Move her ahead of every other patient in the queue
Offer her headphones and leave her in the waiting area
B.why: A quieter space removes the sensory barrier while her clinical priority is kept, so she is not disadvantaged.

whyNot.0: Sending her outside alone may be unsafe and does not ensure she is seen.
whyNot.2: Clinical priority still applies; the adjustment is to the environment.
whyNot.3: Headphones may help a little, but the crowded area remains the barrier.

C.q: Jasmine, 34, has a profound learning disability and lacks capacity to consent to dental treatment. She needs an extraction under general anaesthetic. She also needs blood tests and an ear check, which she has not tolerated awake. What should the team plan?
options: Do the extraction and book the other tests separately
Ask her parents to consent to all the procedures
Plan, in her best interests, to do the other checks then
Postpone everything until she can tolerate tests awake
C.why: Combining needed procedures under one anaesthetic, decided in her best interests with family consulted, avoids repeated distress and risk.

whyNot.0: Separate bookings may mean the tests never happen or need another anaesthetic.
whyNot.1: Parents cannot consent for an adult; it is a best interests decision.
whyNot.3: Postponing leaves her pain untreated and checks undone.

C.q: A nurse is adjusting a children's clinic for autistic young people following NICE CG170. Which environmental change does the guideline support?
options: Brighter overhead lighting so staff can see well
Background music to mask clinic noise
Attention to lighting, noise levels and wall colours
Busy wall displays to distract during waiting
C.why: CG170 1.1.9 recommends adjusting the environment, including lighting, noise levels and wall colours, plus visual supports and personal space.

whyNot.0: Bright lighting can increase sensory distress.
whyNot.1: Added background noise can increase sensory load.
whyNot.3: Busy displays can add to sensory overload.

C.q: Callum, 20, has a moderate learning disability and is very anxious in new places. He needs an MRI scan next week. Which preparation is most likely to help him?
options: Tell him about the scan on the morning it happens
Show him written instructions in standard print
Arrange sedation without first trying other preparation
A pre-visit and a social story with photos of the scanner
C.why: A pre-visit and a social story with photos make the unfamiliar familiar and predictable, reducing anxiety.

whyNot.0: Late notice increases anxiety for someone who struggles with the unfamiliar.
whyNot.1: Standard print may be inaccessible to him.
whyNot.2: Sedation should not be the first step before less restrictive preparation.

reteach.title: Change the service, not the person
reteach.question: How do you check that an idea is really a reasonable adjustment?

blocks.body: If the service changes (a different time, a quiet room, an easy read letter, a carer staying), it is an adjustment. If the person is asked to cope (arrive early, sit still, take a sedative), the barrier is still there. Plan it ahead, record it so it is used again, and do not charge for it.

blocks.text: A carer staying supports care but does not replace the nurse's responsibility.

explain.body: Equality Act s20: reasonable adjustments are a duty, anticipatory for services, and cannot be charged to the disabled person.

test.q: Which statement about reasonable adjustments in NHS services is correct?
options: They are offered once a patient makes a formal request
They are planned in advance and free to the person
They are a goodwill gesture at the manager's discretion
They are funded by the person's personal budget
test.why: For services the duty is anticipatory and the disabled person cannot be charged (s20(7), Sch 2).

whyNot.0: The duty does not wait for a formal request.
whyNot.2: Adjustments are a legal duty, not goodwill.
whyNot.3: The person must not be charged for adjustments.

explain.body: First or last appointments, longer slots, quiet waiting areas or side rooms, and attention to lighting, noise and wall colours (NICE CG170 1.1.9-1.1.10 for autistic children and young people; CG142 1.1.8 for autistic adults).

test.q: Why is a first or last appointment of the day a useful adjustment for many people with a learning disability?
options: It reduces waiting in busy areas
It means a senior doctor will attend
It shortens the length of the appointment
It lets staff skip the usual checks
test.why: Appointments at the start or end of the day minimise waiting and crowds; NICE CG170 1.1.10 gives this example for autistic children and young people.

whyNot.1: Timing does not determine the clinician's grade.
whyNot.2: The aim is less waiting, not a shorter appointment.

explain.body: LD liaison nurses plan admissions and support wards. Familiar carers can stay, including overnight, with their role agreed. The nurse keeps responsibility for care.

test.q: A ward is told that Mo, who has a learning disability, will be admitted next month for surgery. Who is best placed to coordinate his adjustments with the ward?
options: The hospital's LD liaison nurse
The hospital chaplaincy team
The ward's discharge coordinator
The hospital's patient advice service
test.why: Learning disability liaison nurses help wards plan admissions and adjustments in advance.

whyNot.1: Chaplains offer spiritual support, not admission planning.
whyNot.2: Discharge coordinators focus on leaving hospital.
whyNot.3: The advice service handles concerns and complaints.

explain.body: Pre-admission visits, photos and social stories make places predictable. Graded desensitisation helps with needles and equipment. Combining procedures under one anaesthetic can be planned in best interests.

test.q: What does graded desensitisation for a blood test involve?
options: Holding the person still so the test is quick
Giving a sedative before each attempt
Small, practised steps towards the test over time
Taking the sample while the person is asleep
test.why: Desensitisation builds familiarity in small steps (seeing, touching, practising), often with numbing cream, so the person can choose to have the test.

whyNot.3: Taking blood from a sleeping person without consent or a best interests decision is not desensitisation.
